<reason>Side B (PRO) won a high-quality exchange. The decisive clash was whether "one estate, one transfer" collapses digital markets: PRO's distinction between voluntary/repeatable/immediate resale and involuntary, once-per-lifetime, non-duplicating inheritance was intuitive, repeated under pressure, and crystallized memorably in closing ("death is the friction"). CON's friction rejoinder (immortal zero-cost copy vs. degrading paperbacks) was CON's best moment, but PRO's answer that the motion itself supplies the friction held up. CON's retroactivity and next-of-kin points received principled answers (adhesion terms contradicting the headline "Buy" representation; stopping point written into the motion). CON's "self-defeating statute" framing rested on a selective quotation — dropping PRO's qualifier "under CON's own account" from B4.1, which changed the meaning — and PRO's actual answer (if there was never anything to inherit, the statute destroys nothing; it forces honest tiered pricing) survived. CON also incurred execution costs: two clipped speeches (opening and rebuttal 2), including a truncated remedy argument, and a slightly misleading claim in closing that PRO "never rebutted" the chain point when B5.2 directly addressed it. PRO's windfall framing ("paid in full in 2014, gets the goods back in 2064") and the recurring daughter-with-900-ebooks example gave the case a clear, human stake that CON's consumer-law alternative ("a shrug") never fully matched.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The subscription-flight exchange: CON pressed that PRO's own predicted publisher response leaves heirs with nothing; PRO's B4.1 retort — that under CON's own account there was never anything to inherit, so the statute only moves disclosure from after the funeral to before the purchase, and that a buy-tier/rent-tier split is likelier than total flight — turned CON's strongest apparent concession into a dilemma that PRO then weaponized in B4.5 (permanent purchase vs. admitted "Buy"-button lie).</best_rebuttal>
